text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.
White sugar futures in London ended easier in quiet directionless trade. May lost $3.20 to close at $306.80 per tonne, while August gave up $1.40 to close at $307.00 per tonne.

Raw sugar futures in New York settled weaker in spite of USDA's forecast of a stock-to-use ratio of 14.0 per cent, which means that the import quota automatically goes up by 200,000 tonnes. A burst of commission house selling pushed prices lower with front month May losing 11 points to close at 10.92 cents/lb, while July ended 12 points lower at 10.65 cents/lb. The outer months lost 8 to 12 points. The May/July spread grew to 27 points from 26 points on Monday's close.

INDIA - India's decision to decanalize sugar exports has so far met with only limited success, but foreign sales could pick up as private traders familiarize themselves with the world market, official sources said. The government in February authorized the export of 250,000 tonnes of white sugar in the 1996/97 (October/September) season through the Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA), an agency functioning under the Commerce Ministry. It was the first export authorization since January when the government ended an export monopoly enjoyed by the Indian Sugar and General Industry Export-Import Corporation (ISGIEC), a private company set up by the sugar milling industry.

Industry sources fear that deregulation could lead to competing mills undercutting on export prices and could lead to exports drying up as traders were exposed to mounting losses. Given current low world market prices India will not be in a position to export the originally expected more than 1 million tonnes in 1996/97 and exports are now put that less than half a million tonnes down from 876,000 tonnes exported in 1995/96.

However, production too is likely to remain significantly below earlier expectations with current estimates at around 13 million tonnes, white value, down from 16.5 million tonnes produced in 1995/96. There is also talk of a further reduction of 1 million tonnes in 1997/98. However, even if that should be the case, India is not likely to change its status from net exporter to net importer as there are still sufficient stocks.

PAKISTAN - Production in Pakistan continues to lag well behind last year with the total now expected to reach 2.3 million tonnes, raw value, in 1996/97 (October/September), down from 2.7 million tonnes produced in 1995/96 and 3.3 million tonnes produced in 1994/95. With consumption estimated at more than 3 million tonnes the country will have a significant deficit this season and imports are now expected to be around 1 million tonnes, up from more than 400,000 tonnes imported the previous year.

E.D.& F. MAN - Sugar production in crop year 1996/97 will total 122.722 million tonnes, raw value, down from 123.531 million tonnes the previous year, according to a report released by international trade house E.D.& F. Man. The world surplus of sugar will be 2.43 million tonnes compared with a previous figure of 5.15 million tonnes.

Man said the bulk of the cut in its output forecast, from a previous estimate of 123.54 million tonnes, was accounted for by India, where the crop outlook has changed quite dramatically in recent months. Man added the prospect of future exports from Central and Eastern Europe is likely to keep the white sugar market under pressure.
